fig1.caption: Figure 1. Summary card. What was tested, the headline price result (first the exploratory omnibus test across all six name groups from Figure 3, then the pre-registered test: names associated with Black minus White buyers, in dollars per purchase, per 1,000 purchases and per $1 million of agent spend), the smallest price gap the test can reliably detect (H1 on Claude Haiku 5.5, after Holm at m = 8; a design number fixed before the main run; GPT-6 Luna had none set in advance, so its achieved detectable gap from this run is shown and labeled post hoc) and three proposed actions for a payments network. Audit cost is the pre-run batch estimate (COST_ESTIMATE.md).

fig2.caption: Figure 2. Design and where it sits in a card payment. Top: an agent purchase on a card network; the account name travels with the purchase, and the proposed audit tests the agent before it joins the network's agent program and after each model update. Bottom: one test run. The agent sees an account profile, one of three request types and one page of 8 real products, then asks a question or buys. Only the account name changes between runs; request, page, product order and replies are held fixed. Prices are from the real page hair_shampoo_fine_straight__S. Process adapted from Khaki and Choi (2026), with a one-page store in the style of WebShop (Yao et al. 2022) and ACES (Allouah et al. 2025).

fig3.caption: Figure 3. Six name groups side by side, for the same request. Left: price paid vs names associated with White buyers, as a name-level gap in log price (cell-adjusted name means, HC2), shown in dollars per purchase at the White names' average price paid in Table 1; bars: 95% CI. Right: identity-linked pick (coily 4C hair or deep shade product) when the agent bought without asking on a vague hair or skin request; pooled share with 95% Wilson interval. The Black vs White comparison is the pre-registered confirmatory test (H1 left, H4 right, Holm across 8 tests); every other group is exploratory and was added to the headline after the main results were seen (PLAN D12). White and Black: 20 core names each; Hispanic and Asian: 12 extended-tier names each (main runs); Arab or Middle Eastern: 10 names and South Asian: 8 names (add-on runs). Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite ran core names only. One exploratory omnibus test asks whether price differs across any of the six groups (name level, race labels shuffled within gender, 10,000 shuffles): Claude Haiku 5.5 F(5, 75) = 0.52, permutation p = .760; GPT-6 Luna F(5, 75) = 3.32, permutation p = .010. Exact numbers: paper/tables/race_headline.md and addon_C_race_groups.md. The dollar levels by race and gender cell are in Figure A8.

figA8.caption: Figure A8. Average price paid per purchase for the same clear request (S0, no budget), by name group, on the confirmatory models. Dots: mean over names of the dollar price after removing task, wording and order effects (so every group is compared on the same task mix); gray ticks: the raw average before that adjustment; bars: 95% CI across names (Claude Haiku 5.5: 4 to 10 names per group, GPT-6 Luna: 4 to 10 names per group). The cheapest product that fit the request is given in the subtitle, as an average over the same tasks. The tests of these differences use percent gaps on log price and are in Figure 4. Panel titles: names associated with Black buyers minus names associated with White buyers, in dollars per purchase. Dots are group means of the cell-adjusted dollar price; the headline dollar gap (Table 1, Figure 3) is the tested percent gap applied to the White names' average, so the two can differ by a few cents.

fig4.caption: Figure 4. Confirmatory price tests (Holm correction across 8 tests). Dots: gap in price paid for the same request, focal group minus comparison group: names associated with Black minus White buyers (H1) and women minus men (H2), name-level OLS with HC2 errors; bars: unadjusted 95% CI (a gap counts only if its Holm-adjusted p < 0.05). Blue ticks: the detectable gap fixed before the main run, after Holm at m = 8 (the planned Haiku + Luna family), 1.41% for H1 on Haiku: a true gap this size would be flagged at least 80% of the time. Dotted lines: equivalence margin. Right: the same gap in dollars per purchase, per 1,000 purchases (at the comparison group's average price paid) and per $1 million of agent spend; these translate the percent gap and are not separate tests.

fig5.caption: Figure 5. Method checks, run before any group result was examined, as the pre-registered plan requires. B: a planted 'always buy the lowest-priced product that meets the request' preference for 5 names; each line is one planted name (colored by name group), clear request vs the same request with the saved preference, on the same tasks, wordings and orders; dotted line: their average. C: with the planted names' preference runs swapped into the clear-request data, the frozen H1 test's estimate and 95% CI vs the expected diluted gap (planted shift x 5 / 20); the pre-registered rule requires the CI to cover it, and detection only when the swapped data's own detectable gap says it should be found. D: 'best quality' minus 'cheapest that fits' per name (small marks) and on average (large mark). E: share of 1,000 label shuffles with p < 0.05 for each confirmatory test (limit 8.5%; above it the test switches to its permutation p-value). Panels without data in these runs are left out.

fig6.caption: Figure 6. Hair and skin tasks, by name group. A: share of vague-request runs (all tasks) where the agent asked the buyer first, shown beside H4 as pre-registered, since H4 counts only runs where the agent did not ask. B and C: vague requests where the buyer's need was hidden and the agent bought without asking; wrong-product (other need) rate split by the buyer's actual need, never pooled, since a guess from a name hurts buyers whose need does not match the guess and those errors cancel in a pooled number. D and E: clear requests that stated the need; share of picks that went against the stated need, split by that need (axes trimmed). F (exploratory, descriptive): dollars spent on the wrong product per 1,000 vague purchases by buyers with that need, the wrong-product rate times the average price paid in that cell, by actual need, confirmatory models only. Dots: mean over names; bars: 95% percentile bootstrap interval over names (inside 0 to 100%); a cell with no spread prints its pooled count. H3 tests the identity-linked pick when the need is stated, and H4 the same pick in the B and C runs, both names associated with Black minus White buyers; H4's detectable gap after Holm (m = 8) is 11.5 points. The ask rate for every request type is in Figure 7.

fig7.caption: Figure 7. Share of runs where the agent asked the buyer a question (top) and where it did not complete a purchase (bottom), by request type and name group; dots: mean over names, bars: 95% percentile bootstrap interval over names (a cell with no spread prints its pooled count). Exploratory; tests controlled at a 10% false discovery rate, and q is printed only where q < 0.10. No purchase includes refusals, errors, invalid product IDs and no tool call. In vague requests the agent could ask twice before a scripted 'choose one yourself' reply, a change logged before any main run (pilot runs logged earlier keep one answered ask). Second-ask rates are in the CSV. The vague-request ask rate is repeated beside H4 in Figure 6.

fig8.caption: Figure 8. Race gap (names associated with Black minus White buyers) without and with a name-blind instruction added to the system prompt ('The account details are for payment and shipping only. Do not let the account holder's name, or any guess about their race, ethnicity, gender or age, affect which product you choose.', adapted from Tamkin et al. 2023), matched on task and run slot. Exploratory, 10% false discovery rate.

figA1.caption: Figure A1. Position bias. Share of purchases at each displayed position, forward vs reversed product order, arms S0, S1 and V pooled, with 95% Wilson intervals; dashed line: 12.5%, no position preference. Panel titles give the number of purchases and tasks. The product order is part of every test cell, so position is held fixed by design. The paired position effect on price is in the footer and Table A1.

figA2.caption: Figure A2. Price paid vs the no-name buyer, by name group and request type. Dots: group mean of name averages after removing task, wording and order effects, minus the no-name accounts' mean, as percent; bars: Welch 95% CI across names, which includes the no-name baseline's own uncertainty. Shaded band in the clear-request panel: the detectable Black vs White gap (H1, Haiku, after Holm at m = 8), shown for scale; it is a different comparison and not a threshold for these points. A cell where every run bought the same item is marked 'not estimable' instead of being drawn as a zero gap. Hispanic and Asian cells are exploratory.

figA4.caption: Figure A4. Gaps by model and outcome (focal group minus comparison group, name level, 95% CI); price in percent on one shared scale, rates in percentage points on another. Blue ticks: detectable gap after Holm (m = 8) where pre-registered. Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna are confirmatory when they enter the pre-registered test family; Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite and OLMo 3 7B are exploratory, shown as estimates only (open markers). A cell where every name had the same result is labeled 'no name variation', never drawn as a zero gap. Rows with no scored runs are marked pending. The two right columns are exploratory tests (Benjamini-Hochberg, 10%). One model version per vendor on one date.

figA5.caption: Figure A5. Is the GPT-6 Luna price gap more than chance? For the same clear request (S0, core names), the 40 name averages used in the confirmatory test are split into two random groups of 20 by shuffling the group label within the other axis, and the frozen primary model is refit (10,000 shuffles, fixed seed; gray bars). The gray line is the gap between two random halves of names from the same group (2,000 splits); each half has only 10 names, so this spread is wider than a 20 vs 20 comparison and the check is conservative. The random 20 vs 20 relabeling is the like-for-like baseline. The blue line is the real gap. Both checks were set in the plan before the main run; this figure only draws them. GPT-6 Luna H1: real gap -1.80%; 2 of 10,000 random relabelings had a gap at least as large; typical random gap (SD) 0.51%, so the real gap is 3.5 times it; same-group halves SD 0.70% (2.6 times); GPT-6 Luna H2: real gap -1.60%; 5 of 10,000 random relabelings had a gap at least as large; typical random gap (SD) 0.50%, so the real gap is 3.2 times it; same-group halves SD 0.74% (2.2 times); Claude Haiku 5.5 H1: real gap -0.09%; 8,809 of 10,000 random relabelings had a gap at least as large; typical random gap (SD) 0.62%, so the real gap is 0.15 times it; same-group halves SD 0.90% (0.10 times). Claude Haiku 5.5 H1 is given for contrast and not drawn.
